She has a 2-year history of complex partial seizures treated with carbamazepine. One week ago, she developed fever and received erythromycin for pharyngitis. Her brother has attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder treated with methyllphenidate. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). She appears sleepy. Ocular movements appear full. She has no weakness, but is moderately ataxic. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her current symptoms?
correctExplanation: Carbamazepine is a common antiepileptic medication. It has been shown to interact with other medications and caution should be exercised when choosing concomitant medications for treating patients. It is a CYP450 inducer, which may increase hepatic clearance of some medications (eg, warfarin, phenytoin, valproic acid), leading to subtherapeutic concentrations in the serum. Other drugs, such as erythromycin, can interfere with the hepatic metabolism of carbamazepine by inhibiting CYP450 enzymes, leading to decreased carbamazepine clearance, increased serum concentration, and toxicity. Carbamazepine toxicity typically presents with altered mental status, drowsiness, ataxia, nystagmus, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis can be made by measuring a serum carbamazepine concentration above therapeutic levels, and there is a dose-dependent effect on neurologic depression. Treatment is supportive, with benzodiazepines for seizures or agitation, and involves discontinuation of offending medications.

Children with astrocytomas can present with headache, nausea, vomiting, irritability, behaviora l changes, impaired coordination, and visual impairment, depending on the size and location of the astrocytoma. Typical allergic reactions to medications, including erythromycin (Choice C), would present with rash, urticaria, and, if severe, signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis such as oropharyngeal, lip, or tongue swelling; voice changes; wheezing; shortness of breath; vomiting; or other gastrointestinal disturbances. questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of progressive billateral leg pain over the past year. The pain is located on the posterior aspect of the thighs and calves, occurs only when he is standing, and resolv,es within 30 seconds of sitting or lying down. He has noticed that the pain is less intense if he leans on something as he walks, such as a grocery cart. He can still ride an exercise bicycle without developing any pain. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia , and a small abdomina l aortic aneurysm. He had a left carotid endarterectomy 3 years ago after several transient ischemic attacks in the left hemisphere. Medications include lisinopril, lovastat in, and aspirin. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 110 kg (242 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m 2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Examination shows a right femora l bruit and diminished pedal pulses. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's lower extremity pain?
correctExplanation: The patient's symptoms are most consistent with neurogenic claudication caused by lumbar spinal stenosis. Spinal stenosis describes narrowing of the central canal, neural foramen, or lateral recesses of the spine with consequent nerve compression. Common causes include degenerative arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, degenerative disc disease, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and osteophyte formation in the facet joints. Neurogenic claudication describes lower back pain with radiation to the buttocks and lower extremities that results from increased nerve compression, as may occur with extension of the spine during standing and walking downhill. Lengthening the spinal column with spinal flexion as during sitting, walking uphill, or leaning against a grocery cart, tends to relieve the pain. Diagnostic evaluation involves x-rays followed by MRI of the lumbar spine to evaluate the degree of spinal stenosis and whether surgica l management is necessary.

Cerebrovascular disease (Choice A) is a concern in this patient with multiple risk factors and a history of transient ischemic attacks; however, progressive bilatera l leg pain that is worsened or relieved by postural changes is more consistent with lumbar spinal stenosis. Persistent or new motor or sensory deficits would be more concerning for cerebrovascular disease. Lumbosacra l plexopathy (Choice C) describes a diverse range of motor and sensory disturbances to the lower extremities, including weakness, paresis, pain, numbness, and tingling, resulting from lesions of the lumbosacra l plexus. questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of dribbling fluid from her mouth every time she drinks. She has not had difficulty swallowing or any other symptoms. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has an active lifestyle . Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows drooping of the lower lip on the left. The left forehead does not wrinkle on upward gaze. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Bell palsy refers to a facial nerve palsy that leads to unilatera l facial paralysis. It is most commonly caused by viral-mediated inflammation or immune reaction in the setting of a herpes simplex or herpes zoster infection, although it can also be idiopathic or caused by other viral infections. It presents acutely with unilateral facial paralysis that includes the forehead, consistent with its lower motoneuron pathologic involvement. It can also be associated with loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and decreased lacrimation. Symptoms typically peak around 3 weeks, with slow recovery beginning within 6 months. Diagnosis is most common ly based on clinical symptoms, but electrodiagnostic tests, such as EMG, and imaging of the face and head can be utilized if the diagnosis is unclear. Initial treatment consists of oral glucocorticoids, such as prednisone, and antivira l therapy in severe cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Echocardiography (Choice A) is useful in the evaluation of embo lic stroke, since an intracardiac thrombus or patent foramen ovale could explain its cause. However, a stroke that affects the facial muscu lature would spare the forehead. Additiona lly, this patient has no risk factors for stroke or symptoms such as extremity weakness or numbness to suggest this as an underlying diagnosis. MRI of the brain (Choice B) is useful in the evaluation of stroke, especia lly early in the course of the disease, before it may be evident on CT scan. This patient's symptoms are not consistent with stroke. Doxycycline therapy (Choice C) can be used in the treatment of Lyme disease, which may present with Bell palsy in disseminated Lyme disease. Lyme disease also typica lly presents with erythema migrans, fatigue, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and lymphadenopathy, as well as myocarditis, abnormal liver function tests, and kidney injury. This patient has no other signs or symptoms to suggest Lyme disease.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of imbalance and leg weakness and a 3-day history of difficulty initiating urination. He also has had mild midthoracic back pain for 5 months, but during the past 2 weeks, the pain has worsened and freque ntly awakens him. He has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss since an episode of bronchitis 6 months ago. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He is cachectic and appears chronically ill. Examination shows scleral icterus. Muscle strength in the lower extrem ities is decreased in the proximal and distal muscles bilaterally. There is no muscle atrophy, but tone is increased . Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive, and Babinski sign is present bilatera lly. Sensation is decreased to pinprick to the umbilicus. Muscle strength, sensation, and reflexes in the upper extrem ities are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of focal back pain, upper motoneuron signs, and weight loss are suggestive of epidural spinal cord compression caused by metastatic carcinoma. Metastatic disease frequent ly affects the vertebra l column and may cause compression of the spinal cord by extending into the epidural space or by causing bony destruction and fracture of the vertebral bodies. Patients present with back pain, lower extremity weakness, loss of balance, urinary or bowel incontinence, or complete paralysis of the lower extremities. Early detection and treatment are crucial to prevent permanent spinal cord damage and myelopathy. Patients may benefit from short-term treatment with intravenous dexamethasone to decrease spinal cord edema, although definitive treatment often requires a combination of surgical decompression, chemotherapy, and/or radiotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome (Choice B) is characterized by the formation of autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels, resulting in the impairment of acetylcho line release at the neuromuscu lar junction. It presents with progressive proxima l muscle weakness that improves with exercise and does not typical ly present with upper motoneuron signs. Spinal cord infarction (Choice C) may result from occlusion of the anterior or posterior spinal arteries and presents with abrupt onset myelopathy. Neuroimaging may be required to distinguish this entity from compressive spinal cord lesions. This patient's history of subacute onset and weight loss is more suggestive of a compressive epidural malignant lesion. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of buttock and leg pain. The pain occurs when she walks for more than two blocks or stands for more than 10 minutes; sitting or bending forward provides relief within 1 minute. She has not had weakness or loss of sensation. Bladder function has been normal. She has a 20-year history of lower back pain relieved with rest. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus well controlled with metformin. Muscle strength is full. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ except for absent ankle reflexes . Sensation is intact. There is decreased lumbar lordosis; lumbar flexion is full and extension is limited. Straight-leg raising is negative . Peripheral pulses are intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient's symptoms are best explained by lumbar spinal stenosis. Spinal stenosis describes narrowing of the central canal, neural foramen, or lateral recesses of the spine with consequent nerve compression. Common causes include degenerative arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, degenerative disc disease, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and osteophyte formation in the facet joints. Lower back pain with radiation to the buttocks and lower extremities that results from increased nerve compression is called neurogenic claudication. It is exacerbated by extension of the spine during standing and walking downhill. Lengthening the spinal column with spinal flexion as during sitting, walking uphill, or bending forward tends to relieve the pain. The absence of ankle reflexes suggests involvement of the S 1 nerve root.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Femoropopliteal arterial stenosis (Choice A) is a common complication of atherosclerosis and peripheral vascular disease. Patients may present with vascular claudication, which is more commonly provoked by exertion and relieved by rest. Severe stenosi s may result in limb ischemia. A bruit may be appreciated over the femoral artery, and peripheral pulses would be diminished in the affected extremity. Piriformis syndrome (Choice C) results from compression of the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis. Patients typically present with neuropathic pain in the posterior gluteal region that radiates down the back of the leg. The pain is reproduced by flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the hip, which tenses the piriformis muscle. A negative straight- leg test is less suggestive of the diagnosis. questionStem: An otherwise healthy 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of severe dizziness. Severa l times every day she has the sudden onset of a spinning sensation and loss of equilibrium that lasts for 20 to 30 seconds. The episodes begin most frequently after she rolls over in bed or turns her head to the right. Her pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Doppler ultrasonography of the carotid arteries

correctExplanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a common cause of vertigo and is best diagnosed with positional oculovestibular testing. BPPV occurs when an otolith becomes dislodged from the utricle and enters the semicircular canals. Changes in head posture then cause the malpositioned otolith to move within the semicircular canals, stimulating abnormal movements in endolymph and causing a sensation of vertigo. Patients typically report symptoms of intense, brief episodes of vertigo that occur after changes in position (such as after rolling over or rising from bed), accompanied by visual disturbances (caused by nystagmus), nausea, and vomiting. Positional oculovestibular testing, such as the Dix-Hallpike test, allows the examiner to reproduce the patient's symptoms by repositioning the otolith. Further positional maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver, can be used to move the malpositioned otolith to its proper position within the utricle. Patients with refractory symptoms may benefit from medical management including scopolamine or meclizine.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Tilt table testing (Choice B), or tilt testing, is useful for the diagnosis of orthostasis. While orthostasis may cause position-dependent symptoms of vertigo, presyncope, or syncope, these symptoms are more likely to occur upon suddenly standing, rather than while rolling in bed or turning one's head. Holter monitoring (Choice C), or ambulatory ECG monitoring (24-hour), is useful for the diagnosis of cardiac arrhythmia. Cardiac arrhythmia is unlikely to produce paroxysmal symptoms with a positiona l component that is dependent on rolling in bed or turning one's head.

questionStem: A 35-year-old woman has had constant burning pain in her right hand since closing her hand in a car door 1 year ago. Examination immedia tely following the injury showed extensive ecchymosis and swelling. No fractu res were identified, but the hand was placed in a cast for 1 month. She is unable to tolerate light touch or any motion of the wrist or finger joints during the current examination. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Abnormal sympathetic neural response, also known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy or complex regional pain syndrome, can potentially occur after traumatic injuries and has a variety of clinical characteristics. Commonly, patients will develop pain out of proportion to the degree of injury in a distinct anatomic location that does not correspond to a single nerve or dermatome. The exact pathophysiology is unknown but is thought to involve either changes in central pain processing or aberrant stimulation of damaged peripheral nerves that release inflammatory substances such as neuropeptide Y and substance P. Common clinical manifestations include pain out of proportion to the injury with severe allodynia, impaired muscle strength in the location of injury, autonomic changes including increased sweating and color or temperature changes, and occasionally atrophy or fibrosis.

Symptoms include paresthesias in the palmar aspect of the first two or three digits. Median nerve fibrosis (Choice C) can sometimes occur following a bone fracture with injury to the nerve or after surgical intervention. Symptoms include sensory and motor disturbances in the distribution of the median nerve and depend upon the location at which the median nerve is affected. Post-traumatic arthritis (Choice D) describes joint pain that occurs following a traumatic injury to the articular cartilage of a joint. Like most cases of osteoarthritis, pain is localized to the affected joint and worsens with activity but improves with rest. Temperature changes and sensory changes of the skin are not seen unless the traumatic injury also resulted in trauma to local tissues or nerves. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman has had generalized weakness for 2 days. On quest ioning, she reports numerous hosp ital adm issions for abdom inal pain. One episode occurred after treatment of a urinary tract infection with a sulfonamide . Exami nation shows globa l weakness and areflexia; Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick is mildly decreased in a stocking-glove distribut ion, and sensation to vibration is decreased over the feet. She has tachycardia that does not slow with carotid massage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with episodic abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy in a stocking-glove distribution, which is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the porphobi linogen deaminase gene (PBGD). This enzyme catalyzes the third step in heme synthesis, which combines four porphobi linogen (PBG) molecules into hydroxymethylbilane, which is subsequently converted to uroporphyrinogen Ill. Loss of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of PBG, which is toxic to the nervous system. Additionally, increased activity of the upstream enzyme, delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS1) leads to accumulation of ALA, which is also toxic. The mutation affects both erythroid cells and hepatocytes. The disease's manifestations are primarily neurologic and include periphera l neuropathy, bladder dysfunction, and autonomic dysfunction. Abdominal pain is classic and results often from ileus. The penetrance is low, so a fami ly history is not often present, which can delay the diagnosis. Disease flares can occur after exposure to certain triggers such as certain medications, tobacco and alcohol, stress, and starvation.

A histo ry of chronic alcohol intake is required for this diagnosis. Other nutritional deficiencies are often present as well. questionStem: A 62-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of stiffness and pain of her neck, shoulders, and hips. She has difficulty dressing herself and combing her hair in the morning. She also has had general ized weakness, malaise, and a low-grade fever. She has had a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss during the past month despite no changes in diet. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is occasiona l acetaminophen for pain. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows pitting edema of the hands and the dorsal aspects of the feet. Range of motion of the neck, shoulders, and hips is limited. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 110 mm/h. Additiona l laboratory findings, including her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration, are within the reference ranges. X-rays of the shoulders and feet show no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition in which aching and stiffness develop in the shoulders, hip, and neck. The most common risk factors are age (older than 50 years) and being female. It is also frequently associated with giant cell, or tempora l arteritis, which presents with unilatera l headache and vision loss, if untreated. Other inflammatory signs, such as malaise and fever, are often present, though localized muscle weakness is not typically seen. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates increased inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein, and thrombocytosis. Polymya lgia rheumatica is responsive to glucocorticoids, which are the first-line therapy for the disease. Low-dose prednisone is the treatment of choice.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Bursitis (Choice A) is inflammation of one or more bursae and is manifested by pain and swelling over a single joint. Some examples include the subacromial bursa which can cause pain in the shoulder, the trochanteric bursa which can cause pain over the lateral aspect of the hip, and the olecranon bursa which can cause pain and swelling posterior to the elbow. When inflamed or injured, fluid can collect inside the potential space of the bursa causing swelling, which can be appreciated on examination as a fluctuant, tender, circumscribed mass. Muscle stiffness is not a typica l feature. Dermatomyositis (Choice B) and polymyositis (Choice E) are autoimmune inflammatory myopathies characterized by muscle weakness, rather than stiffness, of the proximal muscles. Dermatomyositis additionally demonstrates cutaneous findings including a Ii ht ink- or heliotro e-colored rash on the e e lids and Gottron a ul es on the dorsal fin ers.

questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of daily headac hes for 8 months. The headac hes are localized to the right temp le and usually worsen throughout the day. At times , the headac hes are exacerbated by chewing. She has a history of migraines but has not had one since menopause 6 years ago. She recently divorced and is under a great deal of stress at work. She has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 144/86 mm Hg. Examination shows pain with movement of the jaw and tenderness under the right zygoma tic arch. The nasal mucosa is normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 20 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The temporomandibu lar joint (TMJ) forms the articulation between the mandibular condy le and the glenoid fossa of the temporal bone. TMJ syndrome occurs because of a combination of structural damage to the TMJ and a variety of neurologic and psychological factors related to pain and stress. Patients usually present with unilatera l, dull, occasionally sharp or stabbing pain near the TMJ or anterior to the auricle that is exacerbated by chewing or jaw clenching. Patients may also experience popping or clicking sensations associated with movement of the jaw and a decreased range of jaw motion. Treatment includes physical therapy, cognitive behavior therapy or biofeedback therapy to treat underlying stress, and pharmacologic therapy including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or tricyclic antidepressants.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Bacterial meningitis (Choice A) presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, headache, and nucha l rigidity). This patient's absence of fever and meningismus renders this diagnosis unlikely. Cluster headache (Choice B) are primary headaches that typical ly present with short-lived, unilatera l, severe, often lancinating pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or tempora l region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, lacrimation, mydriasis, perspiration, nasal congestion).

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 6-month history of increasing clumsiness and a 1-month history of irritability. His wife has noticed jerkiness of his limbs when he walks down stairs or walks quickly. During the past month, he has had the same involuntary movements at rest after stressful days at work. He has not had fever, chills, or night sweats. He does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He goes camping several times yearly. He does not appear to be in distress. Examination shows involuntary movements of the right upper extremity, which the patient is able to suppress when made aware of them. His gait is ataxic. Additional testing is most likely to show which of the following abnormalities?

choices.A: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus on brain imaging
choices.D: Increased oligoclonal bands in cerebrospinal fluid
choices.E: Increased serum acetylcholine esterase inhibitor concentration

correctExplanation: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus on brain imaging would be expected in this patient who most likely has Huntington disease, a progressive neurodegenerat ive condition that arises from misfolded proteins as the result of a trinucleotide expansion in the Huntington gene. Patients develop choreiform movements, which are characterized by involuntary flailing motions of the upper extremities. Eventually, these motor disturbances and others, including ataxic gait, greatly interfere with daily life. Concomitant psychiatric disturbances such as emotional !ability, anxiety, depression, and psychosis may also occur in the later stages of the disease. Many patients exhibit a family history of similar symptoms, but the disease can also arise de novo. Since this is an autosomal dominant disease, there is a 50% chance that an affected individual will pass it on to offspring. Anticipation, whereby symptoms manifest at progressive ly earlier ages and/or more severely in subsequent generations, is also typical of this disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Decreased serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) concentration (Choice B) is not correct. High concentrations of MMA are seen in vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which can lead to subacute combined degeneration of the spine. Dilated ventricles on brain imaging (Choice C) are seen in patients with hydrocephalus, which can either be communicating or noncommunicating. Patients can present with headaches, nausea, vomiting, or gait instability but would not typically exhibit choreiform movements. . -. . . . . . . . . - -. . . . . - - ...

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 82-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of difficulty communicat ing. His wife reports that when he awoke this morning, he seemed slightly confused and "did not make sense." He has hyperlipidemia treated with simvastatin. He does not appear to be in distress. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 85/min and irregular, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg. Examination shows mild right pronator drift. During the examination, he is attentive but has some difficulty naming objects correctly and following two-step commands. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is this patient's greatest risk factor for his neurologic condition?
correctExplanation: The acute onset of focal neurologic deficits, motor weakness, confusion, and dysphasia is concerning for a thromboembo lic cerebra l infarction, or stroke. Atrial fibrillation is a major independent risk factor for strokes, and stroke prevention is an essential aspect of management. The loss of coordinated atrial contraction in this dysrhythmia results in blood stasis within the atrial compartment and promotion of thrombus formation. Embolism to the cerebra l arteries results in ischemic stroke. The presence of right-sided hemiplegia and expressive dysphasia are suggestive of a lesion involving the left middle cerebra l artery distribution. The middle cerebral arteries are the most common cerebra l arteries involved in acute thromboembolic stroke.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Advanced age (Choice A), hyperlipidemia (Choice C), increased blood pressure (Choice D), and weight (Choice E) are all additiona l risk factors for cardiovascular disease and stroke. Other risk factors include tobacco use, diabetes mellitus, presence of mechanical heart valves, hypercoagu lable conditions, patent foramen ovale (allowing for passage of paradoxical venous thromboembo lism to the systemic circulation), heart failure with severe ly decreased ejection fraction, and a persona l or family history of prior stroke. The presence of atrial fibrillation in this patient is the greatest risk factor for a stroke. Educational Objective: Atrial fibrillation is a major independent risk factor for ischemic stroke. Preventative anticoagulation should be considered for patients with additiona l risk factors, such as congestive heart failure, hypertension, advanced age, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

questionStem: A 77-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because he has become increasingly forgetful during the past 6 months. His daughter states that his short-term memory is quite impaired, and he says that he is frustrated with his memory. He lives alone and is able to perform activities of daily living independently. On questioning, he reports a 1-month history of a mild nonproductive cough, constipation, mild pain in his hips with movement, mild numbness of the toes of both feet, and a few episodes of urinary incontinence. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin. His wife died 6 years ago. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. His tempera ture is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg. Muscle strength is normal. Cranial nerves are intact. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Sensation to vibration is mildly decreased over the distal lower extremities. Proprioception is intact. His gait is wide based, and he has impaired tandem walking. His Mini-Mental State Examination score is 24/30; he recalls one of three objects after 5 minutes. An MRI of the brain shows slightly enlarged ventricles with minimal cortical atrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Recommendation that the patient move to an assisted living community

correctExplanation: The patient is presenting with findings concerning for normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), with the characteristic combination of dementia (eg, frontal executive dysfunction), gait instability, and urinary incontinence. NPH refers to a type of communicating (nonobstructive) hydrocephalus in which the ventricles are enlarged, leading to damage of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. Signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, papilledema, postural headaches) are typically absent. Many cases of NPH are idiopathic, though some are secondary to a defect in cerebrospinal fluid drainage from the ventricles as a result of scarring or obstruction of the ventricular lining from prior hemorrhage or meningitis. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, although ventricu lomegaly on brain imaging is suggestive. The most appropriate next step in management is a lumbar puncture to assess the opening pressure and clinical response to removing cerebrospinal fluid. Placement of a ventricular shunt may be needed for long-term management.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Recommendation that the patient move to an assisted living communi ty (Choice A) is inappropriate prior to a thorough evaluation for intervenable causes. Recovery of executive function in patients with NPH that has progressed to dementia is uncertain. It may be appropriate to refer to assisted living if the patient continues to decline and is unable to manage activities of daily living. . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 42-yea r-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of intermittent pain and tingling that radiates from his right shoulder blade to his right thumb and index finger. These symptoms worsen with coughing and sneez ing. There is no history of neck, shoulder, or arm injury. His pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. The cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is normal in all extrem ities. Deep te ndon reflexes are 1 + in the right biceps muscle and 2+ elsewhere. Babinski sign is absent. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the dorsal aspect of the right thumb and index finger. Wh ich of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's symptoms?

choices.C: Centra l nervous system demye lination
choices.F: Median nerve compress ion at the elbow

correctExplanation: G) H) I) J) K) Median nerve compress ion at the wrist Radia l nerve compression at the elbow Radia l nerve compression at the spiral groove Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow Ulnar nerve compression at the wrist Cervical nerve root compression explains this patient's symptoms of cervical radiculopathy. Radicu lopathy refers to pathology affecting a specific spinal nerve root that leads to weakness, numbness, paresthesias, and pain in the dermatomal and myotomal distribution that correlates to the affected root. C6 radicu lopathy will result in pain that radiates from the neck into the arm along with decreased sensation, pain, and/or paresthesia in the lateral forearm and the latera l two digits. Additional ly, C6 radiculopathy causes motor dysfunction of elbow flexion and wrist extension, and a diminished or absent biceps reflex. Radiculopathy symptoms may worsen with activities that increase pressure such as coughing and sneezing. Radiculopathy may be caused by spondylosis (degenerative changes of the spine), disc herniation, infection, tumor, demye lination, or infarction. Dermatomes and myotomes are components of the embryonic somite, a paired segment of paraxial mesoderm. When fully developed, the dermatome is an area of skin whose afferent fibers travel within a single spinal nerve, and myotome is a group of muscles innervated by the efferent fibers from a single spinal nerve.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Brachia! plexus compression (Choice A) typically presents with weakness, numbness, and/or paresthesias of the majority of the upper extremity. Brachia! plexus compression typical ly affects multiple nerve roots and motor dysfunction typica lly predominates over sensory dysfunction and pain early in the disease process. Centra l nervous system (CNS) compression (Choice B), demye lination (Choice C), or ischemia (Choice D) typica lly affects major central nervous system tracts, leading to sensory, motor, and/or autonomic dysfunction contralateral to the lesion. This patient instead demonstrates deficits that are localized to a single spinal nerve root.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man with hypertension is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a stroke. Examination shows Horner syndrome and paralysis of the palate on the right. Sensation is decreased to pain over the right side of the face and left side of the body, and sensation is absent to hot and cold over the right face and left side of the body. There is no paralysis of the extremities. Which of the following is the most likely site of infarction?
correctExplanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebe llar artery, leading to an ischemic stroke of the lateral medulla. Five main structures are affected, which include the nucleus ambiguus, vestibu lar nuclei, lateral spinotha lamic tract, spinal trigemina l nucleus, sympathetic fibers, and inferior cerebellar peduncle. Loss of the nucleus ambiguus leads to dysphagia, a decreased gag reflex, and hoarseness. The vestibular nucleus loss causes vomiting, vertigo, and nystagmus. The contralatera l body and ipsilateral face will develop decreased pain and temperature sensation from involvement of the lateral spinotha lamic tract. Horner syndrome may result if the sympathetic fibers are damaged. Additiona lly, ataxia and dysmetria from the involvement of the cerebellar peduncles will also be present. However, a patient with lateral medul lary syndrome may not necessari ly demonstrate all of these findings in equal proportion, as in this case.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The brachium pontis (Choice A), or middle cerebe llar peduncles projecting from the pons, may be affected by ischemic events involving the anterior inferior cerebellar artery. Similar to lateral medullary syndrome, symptoms of an infarct involving the brachium pontis include ataxia and dysmetria, which are absent in this case. Infarction of the midbrain (Choice C) occurs when the basilar artery becomes occluded. This would impact the oculomotor and trochlear nerves. This patient does not demonstrate any eye movement impairment. Infarction of the right temporal lobe (Choice D), depending on the side of the patient's dominant hemisphere, may impact regions such as the Wernicke area of speech and Meyer loop of the visua l pathway. As well, it may impact the primary auditory cortex, resulting in varying degrees of hearing impairment depending on the extent of infarction. Infarction of the right thalamus (Choice E) may develop from occlusion of one of four different arteries, the tuberothalamic artery, . ··-· . ·- . - . - - - .. - . .. . . - ·-·-·· .... ·- - . - .. ... ... .. ··- ...

correctExplanation: The patient is showing signs and symptoms concerning for cerebellar ataxia, including gait disturbance and nystagmus. Other associated findings may include dysarthria, speech abnormalities, impaired coordination, vomiting, and headache. Patients typica lly do not present with a fever, meningismus, or seizures. Acute cerebellar ataxia usual ly occurs following an acute febrile illness in children under 6 years of age. In the setting of an acute presentation with neurologic deficits, CT scan of the head is effective to evaluate for acute intracranial hemorrhage, tumor, or hydrocephalus that may require emergent management.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Re-examination in 24 hours (Choice A) would not be appropriate, as the patient is showing concerning neuro logic findings that should be evaluated urgent ly. Complete blood count (Choice B) could be helpful in evaluating for infection or anemia, neither of which would be the likely cause of the patient's cerebe llar neuro logic symptoms. An EEG (Choice D) would be helpful in evaluating seizures, which are typically characterized by involuntary rhythmic movements, lapse of consciousness, a posticta l state, and may be accompanied by tongue biting and/or incontinence. This patient's symptoms are taking place while she is awake, alert, and following commands, making seizures unlikely. A lumbar puncture (Choice E) would be the test of choice to eva luate for meningitis. Meningitis is characterized by fever, neck rigidity, and headache. While meningitis can cause focal neurologic deficits, they are typica lly cranial nerve abnormalities. In addition, this patient is not showing associated signs of meningitis. - .

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman with a 10-year history of HIV infection comes to the physician because of headache and fever for 2 days. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). Examination shows confusion and mild weakness of the left upper and lower extrem ities. Deep tendon reflexes are increased, and Babinski sign is present on the left. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 4/mm3 (Normal~500), and plasma HIV viral load is 60,000 copies/ml. Which of the following is the most likely finding on MRI of the brain?

choices.A: Diffuse leukoaraiosis with periventricular white matter changes
choices.B: Markedly enlarged sulci w ith genera lized loss of brain matte
choices.C: Markedly enlarged ventricles with minimal changes in sulci
choices.D: Mass lesion within the substance of the right frontal cortex with shift to the left of midline structures
choices.E: Opaque mass over convexity of left frontal cortex with compress ion of brain substance

correctExplanation: Toxop/asma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite. Transmission can occur through the ingestion of oocysts from cat feces or infected meat, direct transmission between a mother and fetus, or from organ transplantation, which leads to invasion followed by dissemination of the parasite where it typically lies dormant. It is a ubiquitous organism and nearly 10% of individuals will be seropositive for T gondii, but the parasite does not usually cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. In patients with HIV infection and CD4+ cell counts less than 100 cells/mm 3, however, reactivation can occur with several distinct clinical syndromes of which cerebral toxopla smosis results in the most morbidity. Cerebral toxoplasmosis typically presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions within the substance of the cerebral cortex, most commonly the frontal and parietal lobes, although single lesions can occur. It is commonly associated with cerebral edema, which may result in mass effect and shifting of adjacent structures. Seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms are common, as are signs of increased intracranial pressure. Patients with HIV and positive toxoplasma lgG antibodies are typically treated empirical ly with a sulfonamide and pyrimethamine if cerebral toxoplasmosis is suspected. If necessary, the confirmatory diagnosis occurs through a brain biopsy, which will demonstrate a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with the presence of the T gondii organisms. Cerebral toxopla smosis is an AIDS­ defining disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Diffuse leukoaraio sis with periventricular white matter changes (Choice A) describes hyperintense signal alterations on MRI in the white matter surrounding the lateral ventricles. It is associated with chronic vascular pathology, such as hypertension, diabetes, and vascular dementia. Markedly enlarged sulci with generalized loss of brain matter (Choice B) occurs in cerebral atrophy associated with age, dementia, and alcohol use disorder. This patient with HIV and focal neurologic deficit more likely has an opportunistic infection of the central nervous

questionStem: An 87-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of headaches over the past 6 weeks; they fluctuate in severity during the day and occasionally awaken him from sleep. He describes the pain as an aching pressure that is worse in the front. His vision is unchanged . He takes aspirin for cervical osteoarthr itis. His son died 3 months ago. He is lethargic and yawns during the interview. His temperatu re is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 88/min and regular, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows cataracts. There is moderate stiffness of the neck with flexion and when the head is turned to the left and right. There is a pronator drift of the right upper extremity. Reflexes are 3+ at the biceps and triceps muscles and knees and 1 + at the ankles. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. He has a slow unsteady gait with short steps. No other abnorma lities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Head trauma, the use of anticoagulants, physical abuse, alcohol use disorder, cerebral atrophy, and malignancy are associated with an increased risk for developing a subdural hematoma (SDH). Elderly patients are at risk for cerebral atrophy, which places traction on dural bridging cortical veins. In this setting, minor trauma such as falls can result in shearing of the veins leading to hemorrhage. In some cases, patients may not report a history of trauma. Patients may present with headaches, vomiting, meningismus, or hemiparesis, or they may manifest upper motoneuron examination findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign). In some cases, the SDH may be large enough to compress adjacent brain parenchyma; the displacement of the cerebral hemisphere can result in neurologic deficits, altered mental status, seizures, herniation syndromes, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. On imaging, SDH appears as a crescent-shaped fluid collection abutting the internal surface of the skull, not bound by suture lines.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Craniopharyngioma (Choice A) is a rare pituitary mass derived from remnants of the Rathke pouch that may present with bitemporal hemianopsia. It is usually detected in youth. Hypertensive encephalopathy (Choice B) may result from acute and severe increases in blood pressure and may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure. It may progress to obtundation and coma. This patient's blood pressure is mildly increased but not severe enough to cause hypertensive encephalopathy.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician because of progressive imbalance and memory difficult ies over the past year. Two years ago, she began to have episodes of sudden imbalance with a tendency to fall backwards. She has deve loped progress ive slowness of thought and movement and has had brief episodes of double vision. Examination shows mildly decreased short-term memory and slowness of verba l respo nses. Downward gaze and upward gaze are markedly impai red. There is marked rigidity of the neck and mild rigidity of the limbs. The gait is broad based with short shuffling steps, and she easily loses her balance, falling backwards. All movements are performed slowly. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows moderate, diffuse atrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy, an atypical parkinsonian disorder, is a neurodegenerative disease associated with tau-positive neurofibri llary tangles in the basal ganglia, cortex, and brainstem. Patients typically present at an average age of 65 years with gait instability, oculomotor deficits (classica lly vertical gaze palsy), frontal lobe deficits, bradykinesia, and muscle rigidity. The gait pattern varies in step length and base width, though patients typically walk and pivot too quickly (as a result of impulsivity from frontal lobe damage), leading to backward falls. Definitive diagnosis occurs by neuropathologic examination illustrating a pattern of neurofibrillary tangles in the characteristic distribution. Neuroimaging illustrating midbrain and/or cerebral cortex atrophy supports the diagnosis. Death typically occurs 6 to 9 years after disease onset. Management is supportive and includes physica l and occupational therapy along with advanced care planning.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebe llar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. Vertical gaze palsy would be atypical. •-··-· - ! ·- ··- ·- •• - : ·- •••• - - -· •••••• - • - -· ••••••• - - ••• - ·- ·- •- •• •- - •

questionStem: An 80 year old man briefly loses consciousness and falls to the floor in a grocery store. He awakens within 1 minute and feels dizzy, but after several minutes the dizziness passes. His pulse is 80/min; his blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg while supine and 150/86 mm Hg while standing. Cardiac examination and ECG show no abnorma lities. During the physical examination , when his head is turned to the right, he suddenly loses consciousness and motor tone. While unconscious, his pulse is 40/min. He awakens within 20 seconds and feels slightly dazed , but this feeling passes after 1 minute. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity syndrome is characterized by an exaggerated response to carotid baroreceptor stimulation, presenting with resultant sinus bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope. Baroreceptors located at the carotid bifurcations and the aortic arch are important in regulating cardiac output and maintaining adequate perfusion pressures to the brain and organs of the upper body. Baroreceptors are sensitive to mechanical pressure; normally, an increase in blood pressure stimulates baroreceptor activity, which activates a reflex arc resulting in parasympathetic innervation of the sinoatria l and atrioventricular nodes, and inhibition of sympathetic vascu lar tone. This results in a decreased heart rate and periphera l vascular resistance and may result in syncope, especia lly in older adults. In carotid sinus hypersensitivity syndrome, this response may be triggered by mechanica l compression of the carotid sinus from external palpation or with movement of the muscles of the neck. Cardiac examination and diagnostic studies are often unrevealing.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complex partial seizure disorder (Choice B), also called focal onset impaired awareness seizures, is characterized by localized motor or sensory symptoms associated with loss of awareness during episodes. Generalized loss of motor tone and bradycardia are more suggestive of carotid sinus hypersensitivity. Idiopathic orthostatic hypotension (Choice C) is unlikely to explain this patient's symptoms given normal orthostatic vital signs on examination. Orthostatic hypotension is characterized by tachycardia in response to the decreased preload, rather than bradycardia as observed in this patient. Vasodepressor syncope (Choice D), also called vasovagal syncope, is common and results from an acute decrease in periphera l vascu lar resistance with an inadequate responsive increase in cardiac output to maintain perfusion pressure to the brain. Common triggers include standing for long periods of time, heat, and intense emotion or pain. In this case, the onset of symptoms when the patient's head is turned to the right raises concern for carotid sinus hypersensitivity.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a 5-minute genera lized tonic-clonic seizure. She has a 1-year history of sudden jerking movements of her hands and arms; the episodes frequently occur while she is getting ready for work in the morning. On arrival, she is confused but gradua lly becomes oriented to person, place, and time. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg. On examinat ion, ocular movements are full. The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ throughout. In addition to valproic acid therapy, supplementation with which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Supplementation with folic acid should be prescribed in all women of child-bearing age taking anti-epileptic drugs, particular ly valproic acid. Valproic acid increases sodium channel inactivation and increases y-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentration, leading to anti­ epileptic effects. However, it also increases the risk for neural tube defects by twenty-fo ld when taken during the first trimester of pregnancy. Supplementation of folic acid prior to conception is effective in lowering the risk of neural tube defects. Patients without other risk factors can take the standard dose of folic acid, 0.4 mg daily, while patients on anti-epileptics other than valproic acid should take 1 mg daily, and patients on valproic acid should take 4 mg daily. Valproic acid is also used to treat migraines and bipolar disorder, and the same folic acid supplementation should be recommended in those cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Riboflavin (Choice B) deficiency may cause cheilitis and cornea l vascularization. It does not have a role in epilepsy management and is not needed in conjunction with valproic acid. Vitamin B 1 (thiamine) (Choice C) deficiency causes variable manifestations including dry beriberi (peripheral neuropathy with mental status change), wet beriberi (dilated cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure), and Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia). Since the patient does not demonstrate any of these findings, supplementation with thiamine is unnecessary. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) (Choice D) supplementation is needed in patients taking isoniazid. Without it, pyridoxine deficiency develops, which is characterized b eri heral neuro ath , dermatitis, sideroblastic anemia, lossitis, and seizures.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man with a 30-year history of alcoholism is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he was found confused and lethargic by his daughter. He appears malnourished and ill. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg. Scattered rhonchi are heard. Abdomina l examination shows no tenderness , a liver span of 18 cm, and a palpable spleen tip. Neurologic examination shows a disconjugate gaze. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Vitamin B 1, or thiamine, deficiency causes two potential syndromes: Wernicke encepha lopathy and Korsakoff dementia. The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy demonstrates encepha lopathy, ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction. If Wernicke syndrome is allowed to progress without treatment, Korsakoff syndrome may develop, which is manifest by retrograde and anterograde amnesia, confabulation, and horizonta l nystagmus. Wernicke encephalopathy develops in patients with extreme malnourishment and/or alcoho l use disorder. While a serum thiamine concentration may be decreased, this is not useful in managing patients as it cannot be checked quickly. Thus, diagnosis is clinical and should be rapidly treated with intravenous thiamine administration.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intensive physica l therapy (Choice A) would not address the underlying diagnosis of Wernicke encephalopathy. Delayed diagnosis of this condition potentia lly leads to coma and death. Intravenous glucose therapy (Choice B) should not be administered until after thiamine has been given in the setting of Wernicke encepha lopathy, since glucose alone can theoretical ly worsen symptoms. Once thiamine has been replenished, then intravenous glucose may be given. Intravenous vitamin B 12 (cyanocoba lamin) therapy (Choice D) may be utilized in the treatment of megaloblastic anemia resulting from vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency. This most commonly occurs in the context of vegan ism, pernicious anemia, and Crohn disease. It is not necessary to supplement in the case of Wernicke encephalopathy. Oral lactulose therapy (Choice E) is the treatment of choice for hepatic encepha lopathy. This is most common ly seen in patients with cirrhosis whose ability to process ammonia from the gastrointestina l tract is impaired. This patient's liver is enlarged, not cirrhotic on

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department after an episode of flaccid paralysis and numbness of the left upper and lower extremities that lasted 2 hours. During the episode, she was unable to see objects in her left visual field. Neurologic exam ination now shows no abnorma lities. A CT scan of the head shows no lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.G: Rupture of a cerebral artery aneurysm

correctExplanation: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction lasting less than 24 hours caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. This patient has developed focal neurologic deficits that resolved after 2 hours, qualifying as a TIA. TIA can be induced by either an embolus arising from a proximal site or from temporarily decreased blood flow to a watershed area in the brain. A hypotensive TIA typically lasts until resolution of the low-flow event while an embolic TIA lasts hours, as in this case. An embolic ischemic stroke involves an event in which a clot breaks off and travels to the brain, occluding blood flow within a cerebral artery. Emboli most commonly originate from proximal vessels, such as the internal carotid artery, or from an atrial thrombus. If the embolus successfu lly undergoes physiologic thrombolysis, blood flow is restored to the affected area and reverses the clinical symptoms. After a TIA, measures for prevention of an ischemic stroke should be enacted, along with evaluation for the potential source of embolus, such as carotid artery doppler and echocardiography.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Rupture of an arteriovenous malformation (Choice A) or cerebral artery aneurysm (Choice G) in the brain are causes of intracranial bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke. Hemorrhage is not a typical cause of TIA and is less likely to be transient. lntracranial neoplasms, including cerebellar glioma (Choice B), frontal lobe meningioma (Choice D), and temporal lobe astrocytoma (Choice H) may cause focal neurologic deficits such as ataxia and dysmetria, social disinhibition, or motor and sensory impairment, respectively, because of mass effect. However, these effects are not transient.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld farm worker is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting while picking peaches. His pulse is 52/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. He has general ized weakness, diaphoresis, and pinpoint pupils. Which of the following precautions should medical professiona ls take while caring for this patient?
correctExplanation: Organophosphates are commonly found in insecticides and exposure to them can occur transcutaneously, or via inhalation or ingestion. Organophosphates bind to and are inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine (ACh), which leads to excess concentrations of ACh in the neuromuscular junction. ACh acts on both nicotinic and muscarinic ACh receptors. Nicotinic ACh receptors are found in autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, and skeletal muscle, whereas muscarinic ACh receptors are found in heart, brain, smooth muscle, exocrine glands, and sweat glands. Resultant cholinergic excess leads to bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, diarrhea, lacrimation, and salivation. Because of the potential for organophosphate toxicity via transcutaneous exposure, medical professionals should always wear rubber gloves when treating the patient. Treatment involves decontamination of the patient, along with atropine to antagonize the muscarinic receptors, and 2-pralidoxime to regenerate functional acetylcholinesterase.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Organophosphates are not transmitted via aerosolization or droplets, thus wearing protective goggles (Choice A) or wearing a surgical mask (Choice C) would not be as protective as wearing gloves . This patient was likely transcutaneously exposed to organophosphates while picking peaches, so wearing protective rubber gloves is a priority. Wearing no protective equipment (Choice D) would not be advised, since medical professionals treating the patient could inadvertently be exposed to organophosphates by touching the patient. Educationa l Objective: Organophosphates are commonly found in insecticides and exposure to them can occur transcutaneously, or via inhalation or ingestion. Because of the potential for organophosphate toxicity via transcutaneous exposure, medical professionals should always wear rubber gloves when treating the patient.

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man with amyotrophic latera l sclerosis comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressive shortness of breath. The shortness of breath is exacerbated when he is supine. His only medication is an 81-mg aspirin tablet daily. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years but stopped 10 years ago. His pulse is 76/min and regular, respirations are 18/min while sitting and 26/min while supine, and blood pressure is 112/78 mm Hg. There is no jugular venous distention. Scattered rhonchi are heard on auscu ltation; they resolve with coughing. An S4 is heard . Abdom inal examination shows retractio ns of the abdom inal walls with inspiration. There is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shortness of breath?
correctExplanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder arising in midlife that affects both lower motoneurons arising from the anterior horn and upper motoneurons of the lateral corticospina l tract within the brain and spinal cord. Neurons degenerate as the result of an unknown cause that may involve RNA processing and/or excitotoxicity. Patient presentations are variable, though typically feature a combination of upper motoneuron (eg, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motoneuron findings (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy) in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Some patients may experience cognitive or behavioral changes, though other patients are cognitively norma l. The diagnosis is primarily clinical but may be supported by electromyographic findings of acute and chronic denervation. ALS is a progressive disease with death usually occurring within 3 to 5 years of diagnosis, most common ly secondary to neuromuscular respiratory failure. This patient's dyspnea with lying supine is most likely secondary to diaphragmatic paralysis caused by his ALS. Symptoms of diaphragmatic paralysis worsen in the supine position, as gravity no longer assists in contracting and moving the diaphragm downward.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Bronchospasm (Choice A) occurs most commonly in the setting of reactive airway disease, such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It typically presents with shortness of breath and wheezing on auscu ltation that is not position-dependent. While this patient may have some degree of reactive airway disease secondary to his significant smoking history, his symptoms are more consistent with diaphragmatic paralysis.

questionStem: A 14-month-old infant is brought to the physician because of four episodes of loss of consciousness over the past month. Wh ile in the office, the infant has a typical episode. Prior to onset, the infant became fretful when his pacifier was taken away. He cried for 30 seconds, then stopped crying and breathing and became rigid and cyanotic. There are no clonic movements and no response to noxious stimuli. His eyes deviate upward conjugate ly; the pupils do not respond to direct or consensual light. Faint heart sounds are heard on apical auscultation; a pulse cannot be located. He recovers without i ntervention and returns to normal behavior within 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Syncope triggered by emotiona l distress in this infant was likely caused by a breath-holding episode. Breath-holding episodes are common paroxysmal events that occur between ages 6 months and 6 years and are typica lly triggered by stress-induced autonomic dysfunction in the form of transient profound bradycardia. The typical sequence of events is crying, followed by breath holding in forced expiration and cyanosis, then muscle rigidity and shaking, and finally atonia and loss of consciousness. The eyes may deviate upward, and the pupils may dilate. Episodes may recur several times (weekly on average). Physicians should assess patients for iron deficiency anemia, which is common ly associated with breath-ho lding episodes, and treat with iron if deficient. Breath-holding episodes typica lly remit spontaneously.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Absence seizures (Choice A) are generalized seizures that cause transient staring episodes with intact consciousness after the seizure. This patient transiently lost consciousness (did not respond to noxious stimuli), and the characteristic sequence of events for a breath­ holding episode would be atypical for an absence seizure. No medications (Choice B) are known to cause breath-holding episodes. Carotid artery trauma (Choice D) may lead to carotid artery dissection and ischemic stroke. However, this patient does not demonstrate persistent neurologic deficits consistent with a stroke. Nor does he present symptoms of carotid sinus syncope which results from pressure against the carotid sinus baroreceptors.

questionStem: A 22-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician beca use she has had a b lack spot that occludes her vision in her right eye fo r 1 day. She also has pain in the right eye. There is no history of trauma . Exam ination shows visual acuity of 20/20 in the left eye; the best corrected vision in the right eye is 20/200. The left pupil is normal; the right reacts sluggish ly to direct light but consensua lly. Funduscopic examination shows no abnormalities. The eyes are not injected . Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?
correctExplanation: Optic neuritis results from autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve (crania l nerve II) and presents in young, often female, patients with unilatera l vision loss and pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. Ocular examination demonstrates decreased visual acuity and color vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect (rAPD), and possibly optic disc edema. Diagnosis is confirmed with MRI demonstrating hyperintensity of the optic nerve. Patients with optic neuritis are at an increased risk for multiple sclerosis (MS), and optic neuritis is a common initial finding in patients with MS. Recently, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) have been identified as a causative factor of some cases of optic neuritis. Patients who develop optic neuritis because of antibodies against MOG and AQP4 often have severe presentations but also have a decreased risk for subsequent MS compared with patients with optic neuritis who lack these autoantibodies. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that a short course of treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds the rate of visual recovery and delays the onset of MS, although it does not impact final visua l acuity, and demonstrated that the presence and quantity of periventricular white matter lesions on MRI imaging is the most important prognostic risk factor for the subsequent development of MS.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. The cerebellum (Choice A) coordinates ocular saccades, pursuit movements, and gaze holding. Cerebel lar lesions do not cause an I• a

questionStem: A 22-year-o ld college student comes to the student health center after an episode during which he found himself unable to move for several seconds after awakening. The episode occurred during the college's spring break 2 weeks ago, when he awoke after having fallen asleep on the beach. He has no history of similar symptoms. The patient is not having academ ic difficult ies, although he admits to recent stress caused by the examinations that he took just before the spring break. His medical history is noncontributory. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency test

correctExplanation: Sleep paralysis, a manifestation of the atonia that primarily occurs during REM sleep, happens during the transition from sleep to wakefu lness at least once in most people's lives. The precise mechanism of sleep paralysis during the transition to wakefulness is unknown, but stress, psychiatric disorders, sleep deprivation, and substance use may increase the risk. This patient's preceding stress and potential sleep deprivation and substance use during spring break may have contributed to his sleep paralysis episode. Patients are typically distressed during the episode and may experience an associated feeling of impending doom. Other features of REM sleep may also intrude into transitions from sleep to wakefu lness or wakefulness to sleep (eg, hypnopompic or hypnagogic hallucinations). Management of an isolated sleep paralysis episode consists of reassurance and education about normal sleep behavior. If sleep paralysis episodes persist, then the patient should be evaluated for narcolepsy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency test (Choice B) would confirm a diagnosis of narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder that involves deficient orexin secretion, leading to the repeated intrusion of sleep phenomena (eg, sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis) into times of wakefu lness. An isolated episode would not be concerning for narcolepsy. Psychiatric assessment (Choice C) and toxicology screening (Choice D) are unnecessary. Though this patient experienced stress, possibly contributing to the sleep paralysis, a single episode of sleep paralysis during wakefulness is common and not an indication of a psychiatric or substance use disorder. --.. -. -. -. . . - - -. -. . atients with a normal standard EEG when the h

questionStem: An 82-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of neck pain radiating to her left hand. She has also had neck stiffness and difficulty maintaining her balance while walking. She has osteoarthr itis, Crohn disease, gastroesophagea l reflux disease, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include ranitidine, cholestyramine, mesalamine, and ibuprofen. Examination shows moderately decreased range of motion of the neck. There is mild weakness and atrophy of the hands and forearms and increased muscle tone of the lower extremities. The triceps reflexes are absent, the biceps and brachioradia lis reflexes are intact, and the knee and ankle jerk reflexes are increased. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. Sensat ion to pinprick and temperature is decreased over the dorsal forearms and hands. Her gait is broad based and stiff. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

He is unable to remember all the events leading up to his visua l loss, but he states that earlier in the day he saw his boss in a compromising position; he is uncomfortable speaking about this and quickly changes the subject. He has not had any eye pain but says that he has a headac he. He has a history of migraines treated with sumatriptan. Ophthalmic exam ination shows no evidence of trauma, erythema, or infectio n. He flinches when the phys ician rapidly raises her hand towa rd his face . Funduscop ic exam ination shows no evidence of papilledema, optic neuritis, or retinal hemorrhage or detachment. A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. On menta l status exam ination, he appears unaffected by his vision loss. His speech is norma l, and he does not have any delusional behavior. When his wife arrives at the emergency department, he asks if he can go home and inquires about when he can return to work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Conversion disorder, also known as functional neurologic disorder, involves neuro logic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient's flinching in response to a visual stimulus indicates a subconscious ability to see and makes a neuro logic injury unlikely. Though the symptoms disrupt daily life, patients with functional neuro logic disorder may or may not be preoccupied with their symptoms. Functiona l neurologic disorder is postulated to represent the subconscious conversion of intolerable emotional distress into physica l symptoms as indicated by this patient quick ly changing the subject when asked about a stressor. Psychiatric comorbidities such as depression are common but not present in all patients. Physicians should conduct a thorough history and physica l examination, and obtain laboratory and imaging studies to evaluate for medical or neurologic disease that may explain or partially explain the symptoms. Treatment of functiona l neurologic disorder involves education about the diagnosis, physical therapy, and cognitive-behavioral therapy.

Viral reactivation within the geniculate ganglion leads to facial nerve palsy, which causes paralysis of the muscles of facial expression (including the forehead) and may cause lagophthalmos and corneal dryness. questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of a severe headache that began suddenly while she was exercising at the gym. She rates her pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale and says it is present over her entire head. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin. She is 172 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 72 kg (158 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. She is alert and oriented. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, the right pupil is 5 mm and not reactive to light. Meningismus is present. The remainder of the examinat ion, including neurologic examinat ion, shows no abnorma lities. The most likely cause of these findings is a lesion in which of the following arteries?
correctExplanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) refers to bleeding into the subarachnoid space. It most commonly occurs secondary to trauma, although aneurysmal rupture is the most common cause of nontraumatic SAH. Patients typically present with an acute, severe headache often described as the worst headache of their life, along with neck stiffness, photophobia, and possible stupor or coma in severe cases. Aneurysms can occur at various locations within the intracranial vasculature. This patient presents with oculomotor nerve palsy, raising suspicion for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Oculomotor nerve palsy is a common presenting sign of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm because of its location and compression of the oculomotor nerve. The oculomotor nerve carries parasympathetic fibers allowing for pupillary constriction and motor fibers innervating the levator palpebrae superioris and several extraocular muscles. Patients with an oculomotor nerve palsy can present with pupillary dilation, ptosis, and extraocular muscle paresis leading to diplopia.

Because of its location near the optic chiasm, it can cause visual field defects such as bitemporal hemianopsia. Basilar artery (Choice B) and middle cerebral artery (Choice C) aneurysms can also rupture and cause an acute headache, intracranial hemorrhage, and/or subarachnoid hemorrhage, but oculomotor nerve palsy would be atypical. Proximal internal carotid artery (Choice E) aneurysms within the neck are much less common than aneurysms of the posterior communicating artery. As well, aneurysmal rupture of the proximal internal carotid artery would not cause cranial nerve palsies, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or findings of meningismus.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of difficulty walking and a tremor of the right arm. He says that his movements have been slower. He has hypertension, schizophrenia, and gastroesophageal reflux disease . Current medications include hydroch lorothiazide, fluphenazine, benztropine, and ranitidine. His blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Examination shows increased muscle tone in the right upper extremity; there is a resting tremor of the right hand and decreased right arm swing. His gait is short based. Mental status examination shows a restricted affect. Which of the following is most likely to improve this patient's symptoms?

correctExplanation: Fluphenazine, a first-gene ration antipsychotic medication, is a dopamine-2 (D2) receptor antagonist. By decreasing mesolimbic dopamine signaling, fluphenazine treats the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia. D2 antagonism in the basal ganglia can cause acute dystonic reactions and parkinsonism, leading to this patient's bradykinesia (manifesting as a decreased right arm swing while walking), resting tremor, increased muscle tone, and postural instability (manifesting as a short, or shuffling, gait). The chronic use of antidopaminergic agents may also upregulate D2 receptors in the basal ganglia, leading to tardive dyskinesia. Management of medication-induced parkinsonism typically involves adding an anticho linergic medication such as benztropine, which counteracts antidopaminergic activity and addresses parkinsonism. In this patient with schizophrenia already on an anticho linergic medication (benztropine ), the next step is decreasing or discontinuing the dose of the offending medication and switching to an antipsychotic medication that causes less potent D2 antagonism.

Benztropine (Choice C) is an anticho linergic medication that antagonizes muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system (CNS), modulating the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia, and thus treats parkinsonism and acute dystonic reaction. An increase in cholinergic signaling through adding donepezi l or discontinuing benztropine would not address this patient's parkinsonism (and in the case of discontinuing benztropine, would likely exacerbate parkinsonism). Risperidone (Choice B) is a second-generation antipsychotic that antagonizes the D2 receptor and modulates serotonin signaling. Of the second-generation antipsychotics, risperidone demonstrates the most potent D2 antagonism and would likely exacerbate this patient's parkinsonism.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of a 1-year history of depressed mood and episodes of daytime sleepiness despite getting an adequate amount of sleep at night. Diagnosis can be made in patients with daytime somnolence and cataplexy or, in cases where cataplexy is not present, with sleep latency testing, which shows a shorter time from wakefulness to the initiation of REM sleep. questionStem: A 56-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment 20 minutes after a simple partial seizure. A CT scan of the head shows a 1.5-cm , uniformly and intensely enhancing parasag ittal mass in the left frontal region. Further evaluation for a primary lesion is negat ive. correctExplanation: Meningioma is a common, benign centra l nervous system (CNS) tumor derived from the meninges that occurs along the surfaces of the brain and spina l cord, often in the parasagittal region. They occur in women more often than men and are associated with neurofibromatosis 2 and multip le endocrine neoplasia, type 1. Patients may be asymptomatic, or they may experience seizures or focal neurologic deficits related to the tumor location. Meningiomas are typically benign but can be malignant. Malignant meningiomas may grow rapidly, leading to symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (postural headache, nausea, papilledema). Meningiomas appear as well-circumscribed, extra-axia l (outside of the brain parenchyma) masses that compress the under lying parenchyma. They demonstrate uniform enhancement on CT imaging. Definitive diagnosis requires histologic examination of the tissue, which will demonstrate spindle cells arranged in a whorled pattern with psammoma bodies. Treatment may include radiation and/or surgica l resection to alleviate the tumora l mass effect, if significant.

She states that the pain is worse at night and is not relieved with acetam inophen or ibuprofen. She has a 10-year history of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis treated with thyroid hormone therapy. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examina tion, tapping the palmar surface of the right wrist elicits a tingling sensation in the thumb and index fingers. Her serum thyroid-stim ulating hormone concentratio n is 2 µU/ml.
