The carpal tunnel describes a conduit in the wrist that is formed by the flexor retinaculum anteriorly and the carpal bones posteriorly. Both the median nerve and the flexor tendons of the fingers trave l through this canal. Increased pressure in this canal can lead to compression of the median nerve, resulting in paresthesias of the first three digits, primarily on the palmar surface. When severe, weakness of the thumb with atrophy of the thenar eminence may occur. The Tinel test involves tapping the volar surface of the wrist in the midline. A positive test, as in this case, leads to tingling in the first two digits and occasionally the third digit, which corresponds with the distribution of the median nerve. This condition occurs common ly in those with jobs that involve repetitive wrist movement such as typing, but it can be idiopathic. It commonly develops in obese patients and is more common in women. Nighttime symptoms are frequently encountered, and the initial treatment requires wrist splints worn at night. Refractory or severe symptoms may be referred for surgical intervention.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found in a state of confusion outside a convenience store. He says he feels anxious. He has not had fever, headac he, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. He has a 3-year history of uncontrolled hypertension. He has no allergies and takes no medications. He does not smoke. He usually drinks 12 to 14 beers daily. He says he has never used illicit drugs. He is disheveled and agitated and picks at imaginary things in the air. He is disoriented to person, place, and time. His temperatu re is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 160/105 mm Hg. Examination shows diaphoresis and trem ulousness. There is seborrhea and rosacea of the face. There are no signs of head trauma. The neck is supple. There is diffuse hyperreflex ia. Babinski sign is absent bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: This patient has developed delirium tremens, a serious complication of alcohol withdrawal. Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of y-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol therefore leads to sympathetic overdrive. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors , anxiety, restlessness, diffuse hyperreflexia, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after the cessation of alcohol use. Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, involves severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability (variab le heart rate and blood pressure with hyperthermia). Delirium tremens typically begins 2 to 5 days after the patient's last alcoholic drink. Delirium tremens is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (GABAA receptor agonists) to address the psychomotor agitation associated with withdrawal and prevent the worsening of withdrawal manifestations. Management also includes fluid resuscitation, nutritional supplementation, and frequent assessment including vital sign checks.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Acute subdural hematoma (Choice A) refers to bleeding between the dura and arachnoid membranes, most common ly caused by head trauma in elderly patients and persons with alcohol use disorder. Patients typically present with a declining neurologic status or coma.

questionStem: A 6-month-o ld boy is adm itted to the hospital for evaluation of spasms. The child's father and a paternal aunt are mildly retarde d and have seizures. The father has acneiform lesions on his cheeks, but without comedones. Examination of the patient shows five 1- to 2-cm depigmented areas on the chest and flexor surfaces of the upper and lower extremities. A CT scan of the head shows a subependyma l calcification near the foramen of Monro on the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder characterized by benign tumors in severa l organ systems. Hamartomas can form in the soft tissue (leading to Shagreen patches, or subcutaneous oval nodules) or brain (leading to epilepsy and intellectua l disability). Cardiac rhabdomyomas (leading to mitral regurgitation) and renal angiomyolipomas are also common. Other typical dermatologic findings include ash leaf spots (hypomelanotic macules) and angiofibromas, which are acneiform lesions without comedones (clogged hair follicles). Subependymal giant cell tumors are common, which typically demonstrate calcifica tion and may increase the likelihood of developing seizures. Though these tumors are benign, patients are at risk for developing malignancies in the soft tissues, brain, or kidney. Diagnosis is typically clinical but may be confirmed by genetic testing indicating a mutated TSC gene. Management requires anticonvulsant medication for seizures and surgica l resection of rapidly growing or symptomatic tumors.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Idiopathic hypercalcemia (Choice A) is a rare condition that typically presents in infancy with developmenta l delay, constipation, polyuria, vomiting, feeding problems, and weight loss. Adults can rarely demonstrate an idiopathic increase in vitamin D and consequen tly become hyperca lcemic. Neither variant is hereditary nor associated with dermatologic findings. Neurofibromatosis (Choice B) is a hereditary neurocutaneous disorder. Type 1 presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), cafe au lait spots, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and pheochromocytomas. Type 2 presents with cutaneou s neurofib romas, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, additional schwannomas of the cranial nerves or in the spinal cord, intracranial meningiomas, and neuropathy. Subependymal brain lesions are atypical, and the dermatologic findings differ between tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis. Sturge-Weber syndrome (Choice C) is a neurocutaneous disorder that presents with the proliferation of capil lary-size blood vessels

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progress ive difficulty climbing stairs, generalized muscle pain, and dry mouth. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia . Current medications include atorvastatin, atenolol, and glybur ide. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. At his last visit 6 weeks ago, an x-ray of the chest showed a solitary lung nodule. Today, his pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg. Examination of the lower extremities shows bilateral proximal weakness and hyporeflexia. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies show an incremental increase in the amplitude of evoked motor response. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented these symptoms?

choices.E: More aggressive treatme nt of high blood pressure

correctExplanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an uncommon neurologic condition that affects neuromuscu lar junction transmission. Normally, action potentials lead to depolarization in the termina l bouton of the axon. Voltage-gated calcium channels consequently open and allow calcium influx, which triggers the exocytosis of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Patients with LEMS possess antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic lower motoneurons, which decreases calcium influx and the subsequent release of acetylcholine. This patient with a smoking history and proximal muscle weakness, with a known lung nodule, likely has paraneoplastic autoantibody production against voltage-gated calcium channels, causing LEMS in the setting of small cell lung cancer. Patients may also have depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. The muscle weakness typica lly improves with exercise as small amounts of acetylcholine accumulate in the synaptic cleft over time, increasing the frequency of postsynaptic action potentials in skeletal muscle cells. This can be seen on nerve conduction studies, as well. Autonomic symptoms such as decreased salivation (and consequent dry mouth) may also occur. The diagnosis may be confirmed with nerve conduction studies and electromyography with exercise testing. In this patient, smoking cessation would have prevented the development of lung cancer and consequent LEMS.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Daily aspirin therapy (Choice B) is used in the prophylaxis and treatment of cardiovascu lar disease, such as coronary artery disease and stroke. It does not play a role in the prevention of lung cancer development. Discontinuing atenolol therapy (Choice C) or atorvastatin therapy (Choice D) would not have prevented this patient from developing lung cancer and subsequent LEMS. While ~-adrenergic blocker therapy can cause fatigue and statin therapy can cause myopathy, neither causes hyporeflexia.

questionStem: A 30-year-old construction worker comes to the physician because of constant midlower back pain for 1 month. He has no leg pain. Straight-leg raising causes discomfort only in the low back. Sensor imotor examination is normal. Which of the following is the most approp riate next step in management?

choices.A: Restriction of heavy lifting until the pain resolves and instruction in proper body mechanics
choices.C: Vocational rehabilitation and change in occupat ion
choices.D: Epidural injection of corticosteroids and nonsteroida l anti-inflammatory drugs
choices.E: lnterverteb ral disc excisio n and fusion

correctExplanation: Low back pain is a common condition that is self-limited for many individuals. There are many causes of low back pain, and it rarely can be caused by a serious illness that requires medica l treatment or surgica l intervention. Risk factors for low back pain include strenuous work, heavy lifting, trauma, obesity, and age. Most patients present with a lumbosacral strain caused by heavy lifting or extended periods of sitting. In patients with a history of trauma or osteoporosis, vertebra l compression fractures or other vertebral fractures are a consideration. Signs and symptoms that increase the risk for an urgent medica l or surgical cause of low back pain include fever, focal midline spinal tenderness, weight loss, pain increased at night, focal neurologic symptoms, and urinary incontinence or urinary retention. In this patient with no sensorimotor abnormalities, the most likely cause of his low back pain is a lumbosacral strain from heavy lifting and construction work. Most patients with lumbosacral pain will improve within 4 weeks with short-term symptomatic therapy, including pain control, restriction of heavy lifting, physical therapy, and instructions on proper body mechanics, allowing for an early return to activity. Prolonged periods of inactivity and bed rest are to be avoided.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bed rest and oral analgesics (Choice B) would not be the most appropriate management. While oral analgesics can help with pain, early movement and physical therapy has been shown to decrease pain and expedite return of function. Bed rest will increase pain and prolong time to recovery. Vocational rehabilitation and change in occupation (Choice C) wou ld not be appropriate before a trial of physical therapy. The patient is young and will likely recover after a period of restricting heavy lifting and physical therapy to prevent further injuries. Epidural injection of corticosteroids and nonsteroida l anti-inflammatory drugs (Choice D) would also be inappropriate prior to a period of physical therapy and restriction of heavy lifting. Typically, physical therapy and rehabilitation are sufficient to treat lumbosacral strain in a majority of patients.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of deep aching neck and shoulder pain, progressive weakness of his hands, and poor coordination. Two years ago, he had a whiplash injury that resolved without treatment over a 3-month period. Neurologic examination shows hyporeflexia of the upper extremities. correctExplanation: Syringomyelia refers to a progressive ly expanding cystic lesion involving midline spinal cord structures, most commonly in the cervical or thoracic spinal cord. Syringomyelia may be associated with congenita l malformations such as Chiari malformation type I, spinal cord infections, autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, neoplasms, or spinal cord trauma. Syringomyelia typical ly compresses spinothalamic fibers decussating in the anterior white commissure. Consequent ly, patients present with deficits in pain and temperature sensation in the bilateral upper extremities and/or torso. (Since the ascending spinothalamic tracts in the lateral spinal cord are unaffected, sensation in the lower body is intact.) Neuropathic pain in the upper extremities may occur. The lesion can expand to compress the bilateral anterior horns (the location of the cell bodies of lower motoneurons). Therefore, patients may present with a lower motoneuron pattern of dysfunction in the bilateral upper extremities (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy). The cyst may progressively expand to compress the lateral corticospinal tract in severe cases, leading to an upper motoneuron pattern of dysfunction in the lower body.
